description: Archive of interview excerpts (finding 1–3). The site hero no longer rotates quotes (Pass 0); this file is kept for reference or future use.

quotes.text: I guess the lesson learned was: do things unconventionally in order to get unconventional results.
I believe heavily in not staying tied to design to do design work. I think some of the best design work happens when you're not under a design title.
I see myself starting as a front-end developer, then a graphic designer — and then shifting toward the role of product designer as the market and tools evolved.
Not intentionally, though. I went to school to study architecture, and I couldn't do calculus, so they said sorry, you can't be an architect.

I grew up as a civil engineer. I never thought in my life I could be in that design world... When I realized that I was focusing during my working day more and more on presenting the project... I said, oh, maybe all the physics and math I've studied wasn't really what I really wanted to do.

I'm probably going to be pretty different from a lot of the people you speak to... I was in marketing and I'm an immigrant. And so the idea of design, it was lucrative... it was really about the financial potential.
I was a designer for five years, I was a senior designer for five years, and now I'm back in school because of all this.
I have three majors. I was professional writing, English and cultural anthropology... my dad convinced me on a whim to throw a portfolio in for the design program.

Nobody teaches you how to be a design leader in school. They teach you how to be a designer. And nobody teaches you how to manage a team, and how to grow and develop people, and how to navigate really complicated client situations, and how to deal with things when they don't go well.
quotes.notes: Transcript lightly edited: merged line break; 'an, how' → 'and how'; opening capitalized.

quotes.text: I did not go to an art school — there was no formal design program at the school I was at.
Now I'm in a strategy role, which I think is still a creative act. But it's worlds apart from what I did right out of school.
It's a tool. Don't forget it's a tool. We will always need someone to address it, to check it, to double check the output.
That wasn't even a thing six months ago. Right? Crazy.

When the internet started, it caused a lot of people to stop doing things the internet could now do for them, but it opened up a whole new world of possibility. I see AI as another cycle, but this one's moving fast.
